name: Resale market flipping

card.summary: Buying limited drops, such as sneakers and streetwear, to resell at a markup, which some people use to fund or access sought-after clothing for their style.
card.note: A commercial practice; resale prices and platform rules change.

quick.overview:
Resale flipping means buying limited-release products at retail during a drop and reselling them for more. Sneakers are the best-known case, and resale multiples for sought-after pairs are among the highest of retail goods.

In style communities it is a way to afford or obtain hard-to-find clothing and footwear that shapes how someone dresses. Some keep what they buy and sell the rest.
quick.how: Buyers enter drops and raffles, or use automated bots, then list items on authenticated resale platforms such as StockX and GOAT, which inspect items before shipping them to buyers.
quick.risks: Drops can be lost to bots, counterfeits are common in the resale market, and prices can fall. Some collectors criticise resellers who buy only for profit.

lead: Resale market flipping is the practice of buying limited drops, especially sneakers, and reselling them at a markup [1]. New releases are called drops, and bots are programs that buy in bulk; rare pairs are often resold for well above retail [1].

For people building a wardrobe, resale makes sold-out pieces obtainable and can offset the cost of what they wear. Sneakers have some of the highest resale multiples among retail goods, and coveted low-production releases can sell for over ten times retail [1].

angle.text: Resale lets people obtain or finance limited clothing and footwear that they then wear.

paras: Consumers began collecting, trading and reselling sneakers in the 1970s, and Nike's Air Jordan line launched in 1985; the sneakerhead subculture took hold in New York City in the 1980s [1]. Flight Club opened in 2005 as one of the first sneaker consignment shops [1]. In the 2010s the market moved to online retail and auctions, and Nike launched its SNKRS app in 2015, which by 2020 mostly used raffle-style draws [1].

StockX and GOAT dominate resale and inspect items before shipping them to buyers; eBay launched an authenticated-sneaker initiative in 2021 [1]. StockX sold $1.8 billion in merchandise in 2020, mostly sneakers, and estimated the secondary market at $10 billion in 2021 [1]. High values fueled a large counterfeit market and authentication services [1].

Bots and proxy servers make it hard for small boutiques to sell popular releases to ordinary buyers, and old-school sneakerheads often criticise resellers who buy for profit rather than appreciation [1].

timeline.event: Nike launches the Air Jordan line [1].
Flight Club opens as an early sneaker consignment shop [1].
